<reason>Side B (CON) won the structural battle of the debate. The somatic/germline firewall (B1.3) directly stripped PRO's opening of its two strongest planks—inheritance and unconsented third-party risk—while conceding the germline case, which made CON look principled rather than evasive. PRO's fallbacks (somatic edits still irreversible; slippery slope to germline) were answered with concrete counters: B2.3's list of legal grave non-therapeutic procedures broke the categorical consent claim, and B4.5's organ-removal example plus B5.1's opioid-scheduling rebuttal showed that infrastructure does not dissolve separate criminal prohibitions. PRO's remaining route was a prediction ("the market erodes the line") without a mechanism, and CON correctly flagged the burden gap. Both sides answered pressure questions directly with proper A1/A2 format; CON's answers (self-regarding consent principle; enforcement-not-ban) were crisper. Execution costs were roughly symmetric (both had clipped turns), though B's closing cited nonexistent "C3.2"/"C4.3" IDs—a minor but real reference error. Net: CON made the debate easier to decide by narrowing the dispute to burden of proof on a speculative slope, which PRO never closed.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.3 dismantling PRO's "consent is never sufficient for grave non-therapeutic risk" claim by listing elective breast augmentation, voluntary sterilization, and living kidney donation—forcing PRO to find a categorical difference between genetic and surgical risk they only ever asserted. Honorable mention: B4.5's cosmetic-surgeon/organ-removal counter to the infrastructure slippery slope, which PRO never truly answered beyond reasserting the prediction.</best_rebuttal>
